# Testing gates

The gates every landing passes, over the tests [`testing`](../SKILL.md) classifies and the
builds [`testing-builds`](../builds/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Regressions

them to its own depth:

  slow list;
- a full run: every test of the workspace under every stage, the slow lists not applied.

  module the campaign integrates; and
- a ship point: a full run, with the coverage measurement.

module pass, so a campaign without review runs neither: they need an owner there. -->

short enough to run each time and no test goes unrun for long. A test joins the list when
an end's run measures it over the minute, and leaves when a full run measures it under. A
skip weakens a gate: the list's changes since the last ship point are put to the user at
each ship point.

BSan, when available, is run for every batch, at a wave's end and at a module's end:

- For a batch, it runs only on the individual tests or reproducers the batch expects to
  trigger it, each by exact name and alone; never on a whole test binary, a suite or the
  workspace.
- At a wave's and a module's end, it runs as a gate over the whole workspace, less its
  slow list, one invocation per test binary, as many side by side as
  [`concurrency`](../../../operations/concurrency/SKILL.md) describes, each under a `timeout`.

cannot finish within that `timeout` fails every time. Such a test is sized for BSan: in the
configuration BSan's build sets, it runs fewer inputs, chosen to keep reaching every path
it checks, while every other build runs it whole.

A batch runs the tests it wrote under Miri. Miri is also run at every wave's and module's
end, as a gate over the whole workspace, less its slow list: one Miri run on the pinned
nightly per test binary, the library's and each integration suite's, as many side by side as
[`concurrency`](../../../operations/concurrency/SKILL.md) describes, each skipping the
compile-fail tests. The gate passes only
with no Miri error: a test that stops at the foreign boundary without the attribute gets
it, and any other Miri error is a UB candidate of the item it touches.

`end-gates`, beside this skill and documented by its `--help`, runs a wave's and a
module's end gates so, over a snapshot of the tree, so that work goes on in the tree while
they run: the format check and the lints with warnings denied, once per export-feature set
the batch checks, the workspace under each variant, Miri and BSan per test binary, and the
slow list's tests skipped by name, each skip checked against its binary's test list before

polled nor read while it runs. BSan reports false positives at the foreign boundary, so

1	---
2	name: testing
3	description: "How work is tested: test kinds and suites, test objects, how thoroughly a wrapper is tested, UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, equivalence and unit tests, and the C tests carried over; testing-builds and testing-gates give the builds, coverage and gates. Read before writing tests."
4	---
5	
6	# Testing
7	
8	Tests are classified by what decides them and by the side of a module they test, and each
9	is placed where the conventions' Testing section places tests of its kind:
10	
11	- UB tests on the safe public interface show that it does not reach UB, mainly by not
12	  triggering sanitizer or Miri crashes, or by failing to compile for a given illegal path;
13	- UB tests on the unsafe public interface target UB there: each public `unsafe fn` or
14	  method a workset adds, called within its stated `# Safety` contract, edge cases
15	  included. Raw `sys::` round-trips are not UB tests on the unsafe interface; they are unit
16	  or equivalence tests;
17	- equivalence tests show that the Rust behaves as the C it translates, mainly by passing
18	  equivalence assertions: `equiv_pub` on the module's exported API, `equiv_priv` on its
19	  internals; and
20	- unit tests show that the Rust keeps its contract, by passing Rust assertions, without
21	  the C: `unit_pub` on the public interface, `unit_priv` on the internal routines.
22	
23	<!-- TODO: fuzzing, of the safe public interface and differentially against the C, is
24	deferred. -->
25	
26	Test objects are constructed through safe constructors. The UB tests on the safe public
27	interface use the safe API alone, their suite forbidding `unsafe_code` at its root: a type
28	that no safe constructor or producer yields yet gets those tests in the batch that wraps
29	its first one. Elsewhere, while a type has no safe constructor, one documented unsafe
30	fixture per type adopts the raw constructor's result, and is replaced once the safe
31	constructor exists.
32	
33	A test exercises the safe API wherever it can, so that the later stages of a port, which
34	keep that API, keep it passing. A test of a C form an item keeps, such as an unsafe
35	adoption, a function pointer's unsafe constructor, a trampoline or an export, goes with
36	the stage that removes the form.
37	
38	How thoroughly a wrapper is tested follows how long it lasts. One a port will replace, a
39	type wrapped ahead of its port or a dependency whose module will be ported, keeps its safe
40	API through the port: it gets the tests of its public interface, which outlive it, and
41	none of its internals. A permanent one, every wrapper of a wrap campaign, the foundational
42	modules' and one whose later stage is held back for good, gets every kind.
43	
44	The builds the tests run against and how coverage is measured are
45	[`testing-builds`](builds/SKILL.md)'s, and the gates every landing passes
46	[`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)'s.
47	
48	## 1. UB tests
49	
50	UB tests show that a workset's public API is free of UB.
51	
52	The unsafe public interface is tested with one suite per public unsafe function or method
53	a workset adds, its inputs built through the safe API wherever one exists. A workset that
54	adds no public unsafe API has no UB tests on the unsafe interface.
55	
56	The sanitizers available are those the campaign built: the instrumented variants of
57	`crustify/artifacts/build.json`, where `asan-ubsan` provides ASan and UBSan, `msan` MSan, `tsan` TSan
58	and `bsan` BSan. A sanitizer without a variant is not available, so no test is written for
59	it and none runs under it. Miri needs no C build and is always available.
60	
61	A target that ships its own sanitizers, because the standard ones cannot run against it,
62	is tested with those instead, each standing for the sanitizer it implements.
63	
64	Each available sanitizer is a separate obligation of an item while it reaches C or unsafe
65	code; once it reaches neither, as a port's later stages bring about, Miri covers it alone:
66	
67	- ASan/UBSan: bounds errors, use-after-free, use-after-return, invalid free, double free,
68	  pointer/alignment UB, and integer/division/shift UB.
69	- MSan: use of uninitialized memory, including branches and addresses computed from it,
70	  uninitialized bytes crossing the FFI boundary, and struct tails or buffers a foreign
71	  initializer left partly unwritten. Its build instruments every component, the standard
72	  library through `-Zbuild-std` included: memory written by uninstrumented code reads as
73	  uninitialized, so a partial build reports falsely.
74	- BSan: conflicting foreign writes and retained foreign pointers across Rust reborrows.
75	  These tests are written like the others. BSan is the slowest instrument and reports
76	  false positives at the foreign boundary, so it runs only as
77	  [`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions section describes.
78	- TSan: races reachable through safe APIs, including every asserted `Send` or `Sync`
79	  implementation and threaded callback.
80	- Miri: Rust-side lifetime, bounds, initialization, validity, alignment, intrinsic, and
81	  `repr` assumptions. Miri cannot call the foreign library, read its globals or spawn a
82	  process, so every test that cannot run under it carries
83	  `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore = "<reason>")]` on its test function, naming what stops it:
84	  `"calls C"`, `"reads a C global"`, and so on. A test is marked only after it was run
85	  alone under Miri and seen to stop there; never to silence a Miri report of undefined
86	  behaviour, a panic or a failed assertion, which are findings. The mark goes once what it
87	  names no longer stops the test, as a module's switch or a later stage brings about. Neither
88	  `#[cfg(not(miri))]` nor test-name filters stand in for the attribute: with it in place,
89	  Miri runs every other test.
90	
91	A leak is not undefined behaviour, in Rust or in C, so neither a LeakSanitizer report,
92	which ASan's runtime makes by default, nor Miri's leak check is a UB candidate.
93	
94	UB tests exercise every owner and borrowed form, shared and mutable access path, lifecycle
95	strategy, generic instance, and callback variant a batch emits. They attempt to outlive the
96	owner, alias a reborrow, reenter a callback, and drop a parent first. Storage that C and
97	Rust both allocate or free, or whose allocator a port moves, is tested for a free through
98	the wrong allocator.
99	
100	When the type system should reject a program, the test is a compile-fail doctest or a
101	`trybuild` case.
102	
103	## 2. Equivalence tests
104	
105	Equivalence tests run the C and the Rust that translates it on independently owned inputs
106	built from one description, and compare:
107	
108	- return values and errors;
109	- out-parameters and buffers;
110	- callbacks;
111	- state transitions; and
112	- lifecycle effects.
113	
114	They use multi-call sequences and compare after each step; single calls are only a
115	baseline.
116	
117	The C side of a test meets the preconditions the C sets its callers, as the wrapper meets
118	them before its own calls: a library's global initialisation, which writes state its
119	routines read without synchronisation, runs before the test's first call that reads it,
120	since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.
121	
122	They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
123	its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves
124	unspecified, such as an iteration order, a message's text, a pointer's value or an
125	allocation count. A confirmed C defect is not copied into Rust. The divergence is
126	documented, equivalence tests are retained for the unaffected behaviour, and the
127	corrected-behaviour regression is a unit test.
128	
129	`equiv_pub` holds the module's exported API to the C strictly. `equiv_priv` compares an
130	internal routine with its C counterpart only where one exists, since an idiomatic port may
131	restructure the internals; a C function the raw bindings do not reach, one with internal
132	linkage, is compared through the functions that call it. A macro that implements
133	logic is compared where it expands, through the functions that hold its expansions, since a
134	test of their callers compares the callers' logic, not the macro's. When no function the
135	raw bindings reach runs any of its expansions, directly or through the functions it calls,
136	no equivalence test compares it: its unit tests check it against the replacement list at
137	each expansion site's arguments, and the batch reports the sites as unreached, until the
138	port of the module that holds them compares them.
139	
140	In a port, equivalence tests are the evidence of a module's migration. While its waves run,
141	the variants still build its C, which they reach through the raw bindings while the ported
142	Rust runs under its own names; at its switch they are retired with the C, and the
143	module evolves as Rust from then on, as
144	[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
145	describes. Only its exports still keep the C contract, which the C tests that stay check.
146	
147	## 3. Unit tests
148	
149	A unit test is the right kind when Rust assertions supply the verdict: `unit_pub` on the
150	public interface, whose tests outlive the C, and `unit_priv` on internal facilities,
151	including:
152	
153	- Rust-only `Iterator`, `Debug`, `Clone`, conversions, and builders;
154	- input rejected by Rust before FFI, including the error and no panic;
155	- deliberate correction of defective C behaviour;
156	- unsafe adoption through `from_raw`, `from_ptr`, or similar constructors;
157	- private or `pub(crate)` constructors and internal destructor/drop plumbing; and
158	- resource release exercised through any of those raw, unsafe, or internal paths.
159	
160	## 4. C tests carried over
161	
162	The `unit_pub` tests the port batches write for a module's items mirror the regression
163	cases of the C tests tied to it: their inputs, edge cases and call sequences, with the

---
name: testing
description: "How work is tested: test kinds and suites, test objects, how thoroughly a wrapper is tested, UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, equivalence and unit tests, and the C tests carried over; testing-builds and testing-gates give the builds, coverage and gates. Read before writing tests."
---

# Testing

Tests are classified by what decides them and by the side of a module they test, and each
is placed where the conventions' Testing section places tests of its kind:

- UB tests on the safe public interface show that it does not reach UB, mainly by not
  triggering sanitizer or Miri crashes, or by failing to compile for a given illegal path;
- UB tests on the unsafe public interface target UB there: each public `unsafe fn` or
  method a workset adds, called within its stated `# Safety` contract, edge cases
  included. Raw `sys::` round-trips are not UB tests on the unsafe interface; they are unit
  or equivalence tests;
- equivalence tests show that the Rust behaves as the C it translates, mainly by passing
  equivalence assertions: `equiv_pub` on the module's exported API, `equiv_priv` on its
  internals; and
- unit tests show that the Rust keeps its contract, by passing Rust assertions, without
  the C: `unit_pub` on the public interface, `unit_priv` on the internal routines.

<!-- TODO: fuzzing, of the safe public interface and differentially against the C, is
deferred. -->

Test objects are constructed through safe constructors. The UB tests on the safe public
interface use the safe API alone, their suite forbidding `unsafe_code` at its root: a type
that no safe constructor or producer yields yet gets those tests in the batch that wraps
its first one. Elsewhere, while a type has no safe constructor, one documented unsafe
fixture per type adopts the raw constructor's result, and is replaced once the safe
constructor exists.

A test exercises the safe API wherever it can, so that the later stages of a port, which
keep that API, keep it passing. A test of a C form an item keeps, such as an unsafe
adoption, a function pointer's unsafe constructor, a trampoline or an export, goes with
the stage that removes the form.

How thoroughly a wrapper is tested follows how long it lasts. One a port will replace, a
type wrapped ahead of its port or a dependency whose module will be ported, keeps its safe
API through the port: it gets the tests of its public interface, which outlive it, and
none of its internals. A permanent one, every wrapper of a wrap campaign, the foundational
modules' and one whose later stage is held back for good, gets every kind.

The builds the tests run against and how coverage is measured are
[`testing-builds`](builds/SKILL.md)'s, and the gates every landing passes
[`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. UB tests

UB tests show that a workset's public API is free of UB.

The unsafe public interface is tested with one suite per public unsafe function or method
a workset adds, its inputs built through the safe API wherever one exists. A workset that
adds no public unsafe API has no UB tests on the unsafe interface.

The sanitizers available are those the campaign built: the instrumented variants of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`, where `asan-ubsan` provides ASan and UBSan, `msan` MSan, `tsan` TSan
and `bsan` BSan. A sanitizer without a variant is not available, so no test is written for
it and none runs under it. Miri needs no C build and is always available.

A target that ships its own sanitizers, because the standard ones cannot run against it,
is tested with those instead, each standing for the sanitizer it implements.

Each available sanitizer is a separate obligation of an item while it reaches C or unsafe
code; once it reaches neither, as a port's later stages bring about, Miri covers it alone:

- ASan/UBSan: bounds errors, use-after-free, use-after-return, invalid free, double free,
  pointer/alignment UB, and integer/division/shift UB.
- MSan: use of uninitialized memory, including branches and addresses computed from it,
  uninitialized bytes crossing the FFI boundary, and struct tails or buffers a foreign
  initializer left partly unwritten. Its build instruments every component, the standard
  library through `-Zbuild-std` included: memory written by uninstrumented code reads as
  uninitialized, so a partial build reports falsely.
- BSan: conflicting foreign writes and retained foreign pointers across Rust reborrows.
  These tests are written like the others. BSan is the slowest instrument and reports
  false positives at the foreign boundary, so it runs only as
  [`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions section describes.
- TSan: races reachable through safe APIs, including every asserted `Send` or `Sync`
  implementation and threaded callback.
- Miri: Rust-side lifetime, bounds, initialization, validity, alignment, intrinsic, and
  `repr` assumptions. Miri cannot call the foreign library, read its globals or spawn a
  process, so every test that cannot run under it carries
  `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore = "<reason>")]` on its test function, naming what stops it:
  `"calls C"`, `"reads a C global"`, and so on. A test is marked only after it was run
  alone under Miri and seen to stop there; never to silence a Miri report of undefined
  behaviour, a panic or a failed assertion, which are findings. The mark goes once what it
  names no longer stops the test, as a module's switch or a later stage brings about. Neither
  `#[cfg(not(miri))]` nor test-name filters stand in for the attribute: with it in place,
  Miri runs every other test.

A leak is not undefined behaviour, in Rust or in C, so neither a LeakSanitizer report,
which ASan's runtime makes by default, nor Miri's leak check is a UB candidate.

UB tests exercise every owner and borrowed form, shared and mutable access path, lifecycle
strategy, generic instance, and callback variant a batch emits. They attempt to outlive the
owner, alias a reborrow, reenter a callback, and drop a parent first. Storage that C and
Rust both allocate or free, or whose allocator a port moves, is tested for a free through
the wrong allocator.

When the type system should reject a program, the test is a compile-fail doctest or a
`trybuild` case.

## 2. Equivalence tests

Equivalence tests run the C and the Rust that translates it on independently owned inputs
built from one description, and compare:

- return values and errors;
- out-parameters and buffers;
- callbacks;
- state transitions; and
- lifecycle effects.

They use multi-call sequences and compare after each step; single calls are only a
baseline.

The C side of a test meets the preconditions the C sets its callers, as the wrapper meets
them before its own calls: a library's global initialisation, which writes state its
routines read without synchronisation, runs before the test's first call that reads it,
since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.

They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves
unspecified, such as an iteration order, a message's text, a pointer's value or an
allocation count. A confirmed C defect is not copied into Rust. The divergence is
documented, equivalence tests are retained for the unaffected behaviour, and the
corrected-behaviour regression is a unit test.

`equiv_pub` holds the module's exported API to the C strictly. `equiv_priv` compares an
internal routine with its C counterpart only where one exists, since an idiomatic port may
restructure the internals; a C function the raw bindings do not reach, one with internal
linkage, is compared through the functions that call it. A macro that implements
logic is compared where it expands, through the functions that hold its expansions, since a
test of their callers compares the callers' logic, not the macro's. When no function the
raw bindings reach runs any of its expansions, directly or through the functions it calls,
no equivalence test compares it: its unit tests check it against the replacement list at
each expansion site's arguments, and the batch reports the sites as unreached, until the
port of the module that holds them compares them.

In a port, equivalence tests are the evidence of a module's migration. While its waves run,
the variants still build its C, which they reach through the raw bindings while the ported
Rust runs under its own names; at its switch they are retired with the C, and the
module evolves as Rust from then on, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes. Only its exports still keep the C contract, which the C tests that stay check.

## 3. Unit tests

A unit test is the right kind when Rust assertions supply the verdict: `unit_pub` on the
public interface, whose tests outlive the C, and `unit_priv` on internal facilities,
including:

- Rust-only `Iterator`, `Debug`, `Clone`, conversions, and builders;
- input rejected by Rust before FFI, including the error and no panic;
- deliberate correction of defective C behaviour;
- unsafe adoption through `from_raw`, `from_ptr`, or similar constructors;
- private or `pub(crate)` constructors and internal destructor/drop plumbing; and
- resource release exercised through any of those raw, unsafe, or internal paths.

## 4. C tests carried over

The `unit_pub` tests the port batches write for a module's items mirror the regression
cases of the C tests tied to it: their inputs, edge cases and call sequences, with the
assertions adapted to the safe Rust contract, so that what the C suites established
outlives them. Each names the C test case it carries over, so that before a C test
leaves, at the module's switch or with the exports it calls, the cases none carries
over are listed, and each is carried over or recorded as behaviour the safe API
deliberately changes. A `port/unexport` carries over every C test case that still references the
export it removes, whatever its subject, as a Rust test of that subject, reaching what is
still C through its wrappers, and removes the case from `c/`.

---
name: reviewing
description: "How landed work is reviewed: tiered review batches and module passes, depth by how long code lasts, worklists, objectives, fixes, gates and plan corrections; reviewing-reports gives the reports, reproducers and disclosures. Read before reviewing a batch or correcting an earlier plan."
---

# Reviewing

Review inspects work that has already landed, for a set of objectives, and files a report
for every defect it finds, as [`reviewing-reports`](reports/SKILL.md) describes. In a translation campaign, it inspects what each
translation batch landed before the waves that build on it start; in an audit, the modules of a crate
that Crustify did not generate (see [`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)); and planner runs review the
plan that earlier runs committed (see [Plan corrections](#7-plan-corrections)).

## 1. Review batches

When review is enabled, every translation batch's landing is reviewed before its wave is
promoted, so that no wave builds on unreviewed work. A review batch is a batch of the wave
it reviews, in `schedule.json`, that `reviews` some of its landed translation batches, and
lands on the same integration branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)
names it. The wave is promoted
once its translation batches and their reviews have landed. An audit's review waves, and
the crate pass that stands in for its module pass, are
[`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)'s.

Review is tiered. Each landing is reviewed within its wave, to the depth
[Depth](#11-depth) gives it. Before a module's switch in a port, and at its end in a
wrap, a module pass reviews the module whole, across its batches: its unsafe regions, its
exports and its tests. It is the last review batch of the last wave of the module's `wrap`
and `port` items, not of a port's later stages, marked
`module_pass`, launched once every other batch of that wave has landed; its worklist is
the module's paths, and it runs the wave's gates and the module's end gates, as
[Gates](#5-gates) describes. A module whose run landed a single translation batch is
reviewed by its module pass alone, whose workset is that batch's whole: a review of the
batch before it would read the same code twice.

A review batch also reads the campaign's lessons that are `provisional`, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Lessons section describes: those its
worklist's commits add or change, and those no worklist holds.

Review batches are packed eagerly, as the batches they review land: one launches as soon as
the landed batches not yet reviewed fill it, and the last once every translation batch of
the wave has landed, so that review runs beside the wave's remaining batches rather than
after them. When a session runs only part of a wave, or part of the scope, its review
covers what it landed, before what consumes that starts.

A review batch takes the commits of translation batches of one route, `type` or `symbol`,
counted over their items: types and symbols are reviewed apart. It is larger than a
translation batch, since its reviewer reads landed code rather than writing it, and is
sized as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Batches section sizes one,
from what landed rather than what is planned: its lines, its unsafe sites and raw-pointer
positions, the regions it touches and the objectives it carries, without overwhelming its
reviewer, and within the settings' review caps (`id: review-workload`) when they set them.
A campaign may also review every translation batch on its own, with that batch's commits.

A review batch's `task.json` holds its worklist, its objectives, its wave branch and its
run fields, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Review batches section
describes. Without `objectives`, a batch runs every objective that applies: those this skill's
Objectives section and the tool skills describe.

### 1.1 Depth

How deeply a landing is reviewed follows how long its code lasts, as
[`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)'s thoroughness does. A wrapper a port will replace, its
item's port planned in `schedule.json`, keeps its safe API through that port: it is
reviewed on its public API, for every objective that applies there, `ergonomics` included,
and not on its internals. An export is reviewed lightly while the C that calls it is
scheduled for porting, and thoroughly once it serves C that stays, for good or when a ship
point releases its module. Everything else is reviewed for every objective that applies.

## 2. Worklists
### 3.10 Test adequacy (`test-adequacy`)

Gaps in the workset's tests: the C and Rust execution paths, and the states and
transitions, that the codebase's external and inline test suites leave unreached, found by
reading those suites against the code and measured as
[`testing-builds`](../testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section describes; assertions too
weak to fail when the code is wrong; tests outside the suite of their kind; and the C test
cases none carries over. A gap is filled with tests, not filed: the coverage measurement
shows the delta.

### 3.11 Revisit (`revisit`)

The reports an earlier review filed, each rerun through its reproducer on the current
tree. One that still reproduces stays a finding of its objective; one that no longer does
has its report updated with the commit that changed the verdict; one that was never a
defect is removed, with the reason in the commit message. Each report's class, and its
disclosure's status, are checked again with it.

### 3.12 Disclosure (`disclose`)

A `disclosure.md` beside each report that is worth sending to the affected project's
maintainers, as [`reviewing-reports`](reports/SKILL.md)'s Disclosure section describes.

### 3.13 Fix (`fix`)

Whether a review patches what it finds. Without it, a review changes nothing outside
its reviews dir but the tests that fill the gaps `test-adequacy` finds.

## 4. Fixes

Under `fix`, every finding of the batch's objectives is patched:

- `unsafety`: the entry point is made safe;
- `contracts`: the `# Safety` obligation or `// SAFETY:` justification is corrected, or,
  when the contract can be broken, the code it guards, and the reproducer becomes a UB
  regression test;
- `ub`, `equiv` and `logic`: the defect is patched, and the reproducer becomes a
  regression test of the same kind, a UB test, an equivalence test or a unit test, on the
  side of the module it reaches. A UB
  regression test either runs without triggering a sanitizer, or fails to compile because
  the patch removed the safe path that reached the defect;
- `ergonomics`: the API is improved, and its consumers in the crate follow;
- `idiom`, `conventions` and `misc`: the transliteration, deviation or defect is fixed;
- `revisit`: every report that still reproduces is patched, as for its objective.

In a Crustify-generated batch, fixes follow the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md);
outside one, the repository's contributor instructions. Every test a review adds is classified as [`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)
describes and placed where the conventions place tests of its kind, or, outside a
Crustify-generated batch, in the reviewed crate's own suite for that kind.

## 5. Gates

The gates [`testing-gates`](../testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section gives a wave's
end run in its last review batch, which launches once every translation batch of the wave
has landed, and whose task's `wave_gates` says so. A module's end's
run in its module pass, when the wave is the module's last: no other translation wave in
`schedule.json` belongs to its module and runs after it. Each runs on the wave's tip
before any change, and again on the landed tree under `fix`. Each true positive a gate
finds in the reviewed codebase is a finding of the batch, filed as a UB report and, under
`fix`, patched, whether or not the workset holds the code it reaches: the gate is the
batch's, and a report it leaves to no one is lost. A BSan report on an earlier wave's items belongs to the last wave's
review.

## 6. Landing

A review batch lands two commits, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Landing section describes: first its
`crustify/reviews/` changes, so the reproducers run on the affected commit, then its
changes to the Rust tree, if any.

## 7. Plan corrections

A planner run that corrects what an earlier run decided files each correction as a finding
under `crustify/reviews/planner/`: `modules/` for `modules.json` and
`schedule.json`, and one sub-directory per tool artifact. Adding what the plan lacks,

plan that earlier runs committed (see [Plan corrections](#7-plan-corrections)).

## 1. Review batches

When review is enabled, every translation batch's landing is reviewed before its wave is
promoted, so that no wave builds on unreviewed work. A review batch is a batch of the wave
it reviews, in `schedule.json`, that `reviews` some of its landed translation batches, and
lands on the same integration branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)
names it. The wave is promoted
once its translation batches and their reviews have landed. An audit's review waves, and
the crate pass that stands in for its module pass, are
[`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)'s.

Review is tiered. Each landing is reviewed within its wave, to the depth
[Depth](#11-depth) gives it. Before a module's switch in a port, and at its end in a
wrap, a module pass reviews the module whole, across its batches: its unsafe regions, its
exports and its tests. It is the last review batch of the last wave of the module's `wrap`
and `port` items, not of a port's later stages, marked
`module_pass`, launched once every other batch of that wave has landed; its worklist is
the module's paths, and it runs the wave's gates and the module's end gates, as
[Gates](#5-gates) describes. A module whose run landed a single translation batch is
reviewed by its module pass alone, whose workset is that batch's whole: a review of the
batch before it would read the same code twice.

[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Lessons section describes: those its
worklist's commits add or change, and those no worklist holds.

Review batches are packed eagerly, as the batches they review land: one launches as soon as
the landed batches not yet reviewed fill it, and the last once every translation batch of
the wave has landed, so that review runs beside the wave's remaining batches rather than
after them. When a session runs only part of a wave, or part of the scope, its review
covers what it landed, before what consumes that starts.

counted over their items: types and symbols are reviewed apart. It is larger than a
translation batch, since its reviewer reads landed code rather than writing it, and is
sized as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Batches section sizes one,
from what landed rather than what is planned: its lines, its unsafe sites and raw-pointer
positions, the regions it touches and the objectives it carries, without overwhelming its
reviewer, and within the settings' review caps (`id: review-workload`) when they set them.
A campaign may also review every translation batch on its own, with that batch's commits.

run fields, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Review batches section
describes. Without `objectives`, a batch runs every objective that applies: those this skill's
Objectives section and the tool skills describe.

How deeply a landing is reviewed follows how long its code lasts, as
[`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)'s thoroughness does. A wrapper a port will replace, its
item's port planned in `schedule.json`, keeps its safe API through that port: it is
reviewed on its public API, for every objective that applies there, `ergonomics` included,

### 3.10 Test adequacy (`test-adequacy`)

Gaps in the workset's tests: the C and Rust execution paths, and the states and
transitions, that the codebase's external and inline test suites leave unreached, found by

=== bsan-borrow-history-grows
PROPOSAL.md
reproducer
# BorrowSanitizer's cost per access to one allocation grows with its borrow history

Status: `superseded` by `bsan-sized-tests` (crustify `c18c8a8`), on 2026-11-14: a test BSan cannot
finish is sized for it, which answers the campaign's side. What remains asks nothing of
Crustify: a report to BorrowSanitizer upstream, the user's to send, with `reproducer/` here.

## Signal

A tool that reports what the source contradicts, here in time rather than in a report: a
loop of constant work per iteration slows down as it runs, under BorrowSanitizer alone.

## Evidence

`wave-225/batch-1/run-1`, the module pass of `src/util/strnlen.h`, ran the module's end
gates on the wave tip `7ef895eb2`. Under BSan (`bsan 0.1.0 (de6ede0149 2026-10-07)`, debug
test builds, `BSAN_OPTIONS=gc_hang_threshold_ms=120000`), `unit_pub` and `equiv` each ran
every test but one to completion, and timed out at 5400 s on the module's two exhaustive
tests, `src::util::strnlen_h::every_nul_position_in_every_bound` and
`src::util::strnlen_h::every_nul_position_matches_the_c` (logs
`crustify/tmp/gates/tip/bsan-{unit_pub,equiv}.log` of that worktree). Each sweeps 8 word
offsets by 2,556 runs of a slice of one 80-byte stack buffer, and passes in 0.01 s plain.

Alone under BSan, the `unit_pub` test kept one core busy and its resident memory grew by
about 8 MB/s (415 MB at 20 s, 1.06 GB at 100 s). The reproducer here, the same loop with no
dependency, run with `cargo bsan run -- <starts> [fresh]` from its directory:

| run | offset 0 | offset 1 |
|---|---:|---:|
| debug, one buffer reused (`-- 2`) | 90.2 s | 420.4 s |
| debug, a buffer per offset (`-- 2 fresh`) | 104.8 s | 103.2 s |
| release, one offset (`--release -- 1`) | 1.6 s | — |

Each offset does the same work, so the reused buffer's growth from 90 s to 420 s is BSan
state that accumulates with the borrows made of one allocation and is not collected while
it lives. Even a fresh buffer costs about 40 ms per run in debug.

## Destination

A tool: BorrowSanitizer, upstream, which this campaign does not evolve. The user reports it
with the reproducer, if they choose to. The campaign's side of it is
`crustify/evolution/bsan-sized-tests`, a rule of `testing-gates` for tests BSan cannot finish.

## Change

None in the campaign. Upstream: collect a live allocation's borrow history, or keep its
per-access cost bounded as the history grows.

## Validation

The reproducer's table above, on this host. The module's two tests now give each offset its
own buffer and sweep bounds up to 24 bytes under `cfg(bsan)`, and finish under BSan.

PROPOSAL.md
# A test BSan cannot finish is sized for it, not skipped

Status: `landed` as crustify `c18c8a8` (record `a44116d`) on `libgit2-crustify/devel`, with the user's
approval on 2026-11-14, which its protected path needs.

Goal: Safety, its soundness measure: BSan keeps checking a test's paths.

## Signal

Review findings and gate failures that recur across modules: a rule the how-to skills lack.

## Evidence

- `wave-225/batch-1/run-1` (`src/util/strnlen.h`'s module pass): on the wave tip
  `7ef895eb2` BSan's `unit_pub` and `equiv` binaries timed out at 5400 s, each on one of the
  module's tests (`every_nul_position_in_every_bound`, `every_nul_position_matches_the_c`),
  every other test of both binaries having passed. Translation batches run BSan only on the
  tests they expect to trigger it, so the module end was the first BSan run of either.
  BorrowSanitizer's cost grows with a buffer's borrow history
  (`crustify/evolution/bsan-borrow-history-grows`).
- Four `src/libgit2/indexer.c` tests that never finish under BSan are skipped by exact name

loop of constant work per iteration slows down as it runs, under BorrowSanitizer alone.

`wave-225/batch-1/run-1`, the module pass of `src/util/strnlen.h`, ran the module's end
gates on the wave tip `7ef895eb2`. Under BSan (`bsan 0.1.0 (de6ede0149 2026-10-07)`, debug

tests, `src::util::strnlen_h::every_nul_position_in_every_bound` and

`crustify/tmp/gates/tip/bsan-{unit_pub,equiv}.log` of that worktree). Each sweeps 8 word
offsets by 2,556 runs of a slice of one 80-byte stack buffer, and passes in 0.01 s plain.

Alone under BSan, the `unit_pub` test kept one core busy and its resident memory grew by
about 8 MB/s (415 MB at 20 s, 1.06 GB at 100 s). The reproducer here, the same loop with no
dependency, run with `cargo bsan run -- <starts> [fresh]` from its directory:

| run | offset 0 | offset 1 |
|---|---:|---:|
| debug, one buffer reused (`-- 2`) | 90.2 s | 420.4 s |
| debug, a buffer per offset (`-- 2 fresh`) | 104.8 s | 103.2 s |
| release, one offset (`--release -- 1`) | 1.6 s | — |

Each offset does the same work, so the reused buffer's growth from 90 s to 420 s is BSan
state that accumulates with the borrows made of one allocation and is not collected while
it lives. Even a fresh buffer costs about 40 ms per run in debug.

A tool: BorrowSanitizer, upstream, which this campaign does not evolve. The user reports it
with the reproducer, if they choose to. The campaign's side of it is
`crustify/evolution/bsan-sized-tests`, a rule of `testing-gates` for tests BSan cannot finish.

None in the campaign. Upstream: collect a live allocation's borrow history, or keep its
per-access cost bounded as the history grows.

The reproducer's table above, on this host. The module's two tests now give each offset its
own buffer and sweep bounds up to 24 bytes under `cfg(bsan)`, and finish under BSan.

# Lessons

Rules that hold for this campaign's target alone, each with the evidence it rests on and
its scope, as the `evolution` skill's Lessons section describes. Every run reads them
before its first step.

## Before `git_libgit2_init`, probe libgit2's allocator only through a release

**Rule.** Before `git_libgit2_init`, `git__allocator` is the failing family
(`src/util/allocators/failalloc.c`), and a test may reach it only through a release:
`git_odb_backend_data_free`, which is `git__free`, sets no error. Any allocation then
fails, and `git__malloc`, `git__realloc` and every error setter report through
`git_error_set_oom` or `set_error`, whose thread-state lookup reads TLS key 0 before
`git_error_global_init` has created libgit2's key: it may return another component's
slot and write `&oom_error` into it. The same holds for an allocator installed with
`set_allocator` before initialisation that fails a request.

**Evidence.** `git_odb_backend_data_alloc`'s finding in the ownership store (ASan
unknown-crash in `git_error_set_oom`, `errors.c:170`); `src/util/errors.c`'s
`threadstate_get`; the equivalence test of `wave-176/batch-0`
(`tests/equiv/src/util/allocators/failalloc.rs`), which compares the C release with the
Rust family's and leaves `malloc` and `realloc` uncompared for this reason. The family's
routines called directly, as `git_failalloc_malloc` through its raw binding, set no error
and are outside the rule: `wave-176/batch-1` compares them so in the test process.

**Scope.** The tests of `src/util/allocators/*.c`, `src/util/alloc.c` and
`src/util/errors.c`, and any test that runs libgit2 before its initialisation.

## libgit2's allocator family is reached through `alloc.rs`'s strategies

  (`wave-169/batch-4`'s `conventions/reftable-error-type-homed-in-basics`;
  `crustify/evolution/reftable-error-wrapped-ahead-of-basics`).
- **Scope.** The batch of wave 217 that ports `enm::reftable_error` and
  `fn::reftable_error_str`, and every reftable module's batch until then.

## A libgit2 module's switch removes its file from `c/` and changes no CMake file

- **Rule.** libgit2's CMake globs each directory's sources (`file(GLOB …)` in
  `src/util/CMakeLists.txt`, `src/libgit2/CMakeLists.txt`, `src/cli/CMakeLists.txt` and the
  tests'), so a module's switch removes its TU, and the tied C tests that reach its internals,
  from `c/` on the fork's `fork/main`, and edits no `CMakeLists.txt`: the C that remains
  already links the Rust's static library wherever it links (`LIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY`,
  `c/cmake/SelectRust.cmake`). A glob is read at `configure` only, so the variants are
  configured afresh, as a new generation (`crustify/scripts/build-variants.sh`), never
  rebuilt in place: a build that only reran `cmake --build` would still list the removed file
  as an input, and fail on it.
- **Evidence.** `src/util/utf8.c`'s switch (`modules/libgit2/src/util/utf8.c/integration/run-1`,
  the fork's `1b37e3d08`): removing the file was the whole C change of the module, beside the
  one-time CMake change; `crustify/builds.gen1`'s archives hold 212 objects where the previous
  generation's held 213, `utf8.c.o` gone.
- **Scope.** Every later module's switch, and every rebuild of the variants after one.

## A `git2` module's exports are checked through the CLI

- **Rule.** No C test reaches the `git2` link unit, the CLI under `src/cli/`: its modules'
  `tests` are empty, and no suite under `c/tests` builds or runs `src/cli`. Its exports are
  therefore checked, before the module's switch, by the gateway's own tests, written after the
  CLI's C that calls them and run with the export feature on against a private build whose
  archive lacks the module's object, and under Miri; and by the CLI itself: the variant's
  `git2` relinked from its `build.ninja` edge (`build git2: C_EXECUTABLE_LINKER__git2_cli_…`),
  without the module's `src/cli/CMakeFiles/git2_cli.dir/<tu>.o` and with the crate built as a
  `staticlib` with the feature on (`CRUSTIFY_STATICLIB=1`, `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` the private
  build, a `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` of its own), then run beside the stock `git2` over the commands'
  usual and failing command lines in scratch repositories, every difference in exit status,
  output or files written either a departure the module records or a finding. After the
  switch, the relinked CLI is the variants' own, and the same command lines check it.
- **Evidence.** `wave-186/batch-7/run-1`, `src/cli/opt.c`'s module pass: its gateway tests
  under Miri found `ub_export/args-slot-handed-to-c-through-a-dead-borrow`, and its relinked
  `git2`, over the 66 command lines of its run dir's `cli-smoke.py`, matched the stock one on 62,
  the 4 others the parser's recorded departures (the bare `-`, and the literal `--`'s
  reordering).
- **Scope.** Every module of the `git2` link unit, at its module pass and its switch, until the
  CLI has tests of its own.

## cmake-property-naming-a-removed-source

Status: provisional

**Rule.** When a module's switch removes a C file that a `CMakeLists.txt` names only in a
source-file property, the `CMakeLists.txt` is left unchanged. CMake ignores a property of a
source no target lists. This extends the lesson "A libgit2 module's switch removes its file
from `c/` and changes no CMake file": the switch still edits no CMake file. The dangling
name stays until the last file the property names goes.

**Evidence.** Item 13 of `module-switch-procedure`. `deps/llhttp/CMakeLists.txt` globs its
sources, as the lesson has it, and also sets
`set_source_files_properties(api.c http.c llhttp.c PROPERTIES COMPILE_FLAGS …)`. At
`deps/llhttp/api.c`'s switch (`modules/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c/integration/run-1`) the
file was left unchanged, and gen3's five `configure`s and builds passed with it. At
`deps/llhttp/http.c`'s switch (`modules/libgit2/deps/llhttp/http.c/integration/run-1`) the
property names `api.c` and `http.c`, both gone, and `llhttp.c`; the file is unchanged, and
gen5's five `configure`s and builds passed with it.

Scope: the switches of `deps/llhttp/*.c`, and any later module whose `CMakeLists.txt` names its file in `set_source_files_properties`.

## http-exports-gated-through-a-local-remote

Status: provisional

**Rule.** No offline C test drives libgit2's HTTP client: `httpparser.c`, `httpclient.c` and
`llhttp.c`'s generated parser call llhttp's exports only in a fetch, clone or push over
HTTP, whose suites (`online::*`) the baseline disables, since they need the network. The
switch of a module whose exports only the HTTP client reaches therefore runs
`crustify/scripts/http-gate.sh` on the previous generation and on the new one, on plain,
ASan+UBSan and TSan, and compares the two `results.txt` with `diff`. On the new generation's
coverage variant, the run also records which of the module's exports the gate calls.
`http-gate.sh` starts two remotes from `crustify/scripts/http-remote.py`, one open and one
asking for Basic credentials. It runs a variant's `git2 clone` of two repositories through
each framing, three clones that fail, and `libgit2_tests -sonline::push
-sonline::clone::credentials` with `GITTEST_REMOTE_URL` at the guarded remote.

**Evidence.** Item 11 of `module-switch-procedure`, met at `deps/llhttp/api.c`'s switch
(`modules/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c/integration/run-1`, the fork's `c54c0c180`). That no
offline C test drives the client is the module pass's finding; the 31 exports are api.c's.
libgit2's own CI runs part of the online suites offline, against servers on localhost named
by `GITTEST_REMOTE_URL` (`ci/test.sh`'s `auth_clone_and_push`, `-sonline::clone::push
-sonline::push`). The run added `http-remote.py`, `git http-backend` behind a persistent
HTTP/1.1 front that frames each response by its path (`Content-Length`, chunked in 1, 7,
4096 and 65536-byte chunks, chunked with chunk extensions, or close-delimited), with an
optional Basic challenge, and `http-gate.sh`, whose `results.txt` is free of times, ports

# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage
under the module's equivalence tests shows how much of its behaviour they compare, set
against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its
Rust's.

#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  asan-ubsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address"
    export ASAN_OPTIONS=${ASAN_OPTIONS:-detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1}
    export UBSAN_OPTIONS=${UBSAN_OPTIONS:-print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  tsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    # glibc's tzset locks what TSan cannot see: see tsan.supp.
    export TSAN_OPTIONS=${TSAN_OPTIONS:-halt_on_error=1:suppressions=$here/crustify/scripts/tsan.supp}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" -Zbuild-std --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  bsan)
    # trybuild's nested cargo build does not finish under BorrowSanitizer, and the
    # compile-fail suite is a compile-time check the plain variant already runs.
    # Under parallel test threads BorrowSanitizer's GC can take longer than its default
    # 10 s hang threshold to bring every thread to a safepoint, and then aborts; give it
    # 120 s rather than serialize the tests.
    export BSAN_OPTIONS=${BSAN_OPTIONS:-gc_hang_threshold_ms=120000}
    if [ "${1:-}" = test ]; then
      case " $* " in
        *" -- "*) exec cargo bsan "$@" --skip compile_fail ;;
        *) exec cargo bsan "$@" -- --skip compile_fail ;;
      esac
    fi
    exec cargo bsan "$@" ;;
  *)
    echo "unknown variant: $variant" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

content.content:
## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

#!/bin/bash
# Drive libgit2's HTTP client through a variant's own C, over a smart-HTTP remote on localhost
# (crustify's testing-gates skill, Regressions: a module's switch, for a module whose exports
# the HTTP client reaches, which no offline C test does; crustify/evolution/module-switch-procedure).
#
#   http-gate.sh <variant dir> <out dir>
#
# <variant dir> is a built variant, crustify/builds.gen<n>/<variant>, with its `git2` and
# `libgit2_tests`; nothing is written into it. Two remotes are started from
# crustify/scripts/http-remote.py over scratch repositories under <out dir>/remotes, one open
# and one asking for Basic credentials (foo:bar), each serving every framing it offers
# (Content-Length, chunked, chunked with extensions, close-delimited, malformed):
#
# 1. the variant's `git2 clone` of testrepo.git (c/tests/resources) and of a three-commit
#    repository of the generation's c/ tree at a fixed commit, through the Content-Length and
#    chunked framings, and clones that fail: through the close-delimited framing, which
#    libgit2 does not read to its end, through a response llhttp refuses, of a missing
#    repository (404), and of the guarded remote without credentials (401); each clone's exit
#    status, refs, HEAD, checked-out tree and `git fsck --connectivity-only` outcome, or its
#    error;
# 2. the variant's `libgit2_tests -sonline::push -sonline::clone::credentials`, libgit2's own
#    C tests of a push and a clone over GITTEST_REMOTE_URL, against the guarded remote with
#    foo:bar, through the Content-Length and chunked framings: its TAP tally.
#
# 3. the requests each remote answered, by method, framing and status, and the connections the
#    client opened to it, by framing.
#
# <out dir>/results.txt is one line per case, free of times, ports and paths, so that two
# generations' results compare with `diff`; every process's output is kept beside it, and each
# line counts the sanitizer reports that process printed (`reports=`). The exit status is 0
# when every clone that should succeed did and every suite passed, 1 otherwise.
set -uo pipefail
usage='usage: http-gate.sh <variant dir> <out dir>'
d=$(cd -P "${1:?$usage}" && pwd) || exit 2
out=${2:?$usage}
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)
c=$(cd -P "$d/../c" && pwd) || { echo "http-gate.sh: no generation c/ beside $d" >&2; exit 2; }
[ -x "$d/git2" ] && [ -x "$d/libgit2_tests" ] || { echo "http-gate.sh: $d has no git2 or libgit2_tests" >&2; exit 2; }
rm -rf "$out"
mkdir -p "$out"
out=$(cd -P "$out" && pwd)
export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-/dev/null}
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE='2026-01-01T00:00:00Z' GIT_COMMITTER_DATE='2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'
# big.git's tree: the campaign's source revision, which every generation's c/ holds.
big_tip=0551dfd4a
framings=(length chunked chunked-ext)
status=0
results=$out/results.txt
: >"$results"
reports() { grep -cE 'WARNING: ThreadSanitizer|ERROR: AddressSanitizer|ERROR: LeakSanitizer|runtime error:' "$@" 2>/dev/null | awk -F: '{s+=$NF} END {print s+0}'; }

# The remotes' repositories.
r=$out/remotes
mkdir -p "$r/open" "$r/guarded"
git clone -q --bare "$c/tests/resources/testrepo.git" "$r/open/testrepo.git"
# big.git: the source revision's tree as three commits, the second removing src/ and the
# third restoring it, each with a fixed author and date, so that its ids are every run's.
mkdir -p "$r/src"
git -C "$c" archive "$big_tip" | tar -x -C "$r/src"

line+=" reports=$(reports "$dir.err")"
  echo "$line" >>"$results"
  case $expect in
    ok) [ $rc -eq 0 ] && [[ $line == *fsck=ok* ]] || status=1 ;;
    fail) [ $rc -ne 0 ] || status=1 ;;
  esac
}
for f in "${framings[@]}"; do
  clone "testrepo-$f" "$open/$f/testrepo.git" ok
  clone "big-$f" "$open/$f/big.git" ok
done
clone testrepo-close "$open/close/testrepo.git" fail
clone testrepo-malformed "$open/malformed/testrepo.git" fail
clone missing "$open/length/missing.git" fail
clone unauthorised "$guarded/length/testrepo.git" fail

# 2. libgit2's own online tests of a push and a clone.
for f in "${framings[@]}"; do
  s=$out/suites/$f
  mkdir -p "$s/tmp"
  (cd "$s" && TMPDIR=$s/tmp GITTEST_REMOTE_URL="$guarded/$f/push-$f.git" GITTEST_REMOTE_USER=foo \
    GITTEST_REMOTE_PASS=bar timeout 1800 "$d/libgit2_tests" -t -sonline::push \
    -sonline::clone::credentials >"$s/tap" 2>"$s/err" </dev/null)
  rc=$?
  ok=$(grep -c '^ok ' "$s/tap") notok=$(grep -c '^not ok ' "$s/tap") skip=$(grep -c '# SKIP' "$s/tap")
  echo "suites $f rc=$rc ok=$ok not_ok=$notok skip=$skip reports=$(reports "$s/err" "$s/tap")" >>"$results"
  [ $rc -eq 0 ] && [ "$notok" -eq 0 ] && [ "$ok" -gt 0 ] || status=1
done

# The requests the remotes answered, by method, framing and status; the connections a client
# reset or closed mid-request (`error` lines) depend on timing, and stay in the logs alone.
# Then the connections the client opened, by framing: a request that is the first on its
# connection opened it, so that a client that stops keeping connections alive, as
# `llhttp_should_keep_alive` tells libgit2's to, opens more.
for side in open guarded; do
  grep -v '^error ' "$out/$side.log" | awk -v s="$side" '{split($2, p, "/"); print "requests " s " " $1 " " p[2] " " $3}' |
    sort | uniq -c | awk '{print $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, "count=" $1}' >>"$results"
done
for side in open guarded; do
  grep -v '^error ' "$out/$side.log" | awk -v s="$side" '$4 == "conn=1" {split($2, p, "/"); print "connections " s " " p[2]}' |
    sort | uniq -c | awk '{print $2, $3, $4, "count=" $1}' >>"$results"
done
cat "$results"
exit $status

description: "How a review's findings are filed: report directories, classes, evidence, conditions, root causes, notes, reproducers, and disclosure drafts with their upstream check and status. # Reviewing: reports

What a review files for the defects [`reviewing`](../SKILL.md)'s objectives name: a report
per root cause, the reproducer that proves it, and, under `disclose`, the draft its
project's maintainers are sent.

## 1. Reports

A review batch files its findings under its reviews dir, as
[`layout`](../../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Reviews section spells it,
each in its own `<slug>` directory, holding its report and, when it has one, its
reproducer, in the sub-directory of its objective:

| objective | sub-directory |
|---|---|
| `unsafety` | `unsafe/` |
| `contracts`, of a gateway | `contracts/ffi_export/` |
| `contracts`, of other unsafe code | `contracts/ffi_import/` |
| `ub`, on the safe interface | `ub_safe/` |
| `ub`, on the unsafe interface | `ub_unsafe/` |
| `ub`, through an export | `ub_export/` |
| `equiv` | `equiv/` |
| `logic` | `logic/` |
| `ergonomics` | `ergonomics/` |
| `idiom` | `idiom/` |
| `conventions` | `conventions/` |
| `misc` | `misc/` |

A tool may add sub-directories for findings on its own output. A defect in a tool
rather than in the reviewed codebase, Crustify included, is no finding: it is a proposal,
with its reproducer, as [`evolution`](../../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Proposals
section describes.

A report states what is wrong, where, the evidence that proves it, and, under `fix`, how it
was fixed. It names the tier that caught the finding, and the tiers that had the same code
in scope before it and passed it. The tiers are a batch's own gates, a review batch, a
module pass, a switch, a later stage's review, a revisit, a ship point's gates and a
consumer. A finding caught by a later tier than the first that had it in scope is an
escape. A finding of `ub` or `contracts` also names the pattern of
[`soundness`](../../../rust/soundness/SKILL.md) it is an instance of, or `new`. A finding that a switch, a ship point's gates or a consumer catches is filed by the
review batch it is handed to, which names that tier. It carries everything needed to rerun
its reproducer from a clean checkout: the exact command and the sanitizer output or failing
assertion it produced. Neither a report nor a reproducer carries an API key, in a core dump
or anywhere else: a reviews dir may be published.

### 1.1 Header

A report opens with its header, one `key: value` line each:

- `class`, as [Classes](#12-classes) gives it;
- `evidence`: what decided it, a sanitizer, Miri or a failing assertion, by name. A
  result that only an aliasing model reports, Stacked Borrows, Tree Borrows or BSan, adds
  `aliasing-model only`; one that rests on a claim the Rust Reference does not settle,
  such as a reference to an uninhabited opaque type or to a partly initialised struct,
  adds `unsettled`. Either says so wherever the report or its disclosure states the
  defect, and neither is called undefined behaviour without that qualifier;
- `conditions`: the Cargo features, target and `cfg`s it needs, whether it needs a system
  C library rather than the bundled one, or a version of it, and the revisions it
  reproduces on; and
- `same-cause`, where another report in the tree has the same root cause: that report's
  dir.

### 1.2 Classes

| class | what the report shows |
|---|---|
| `soundness` | undefined behaviour reached from the safe public API, from the unsafe public API within its `# Safety` obligations, or by C through an export within the C declaration's contract |
| `c-bug` | a defect of the C library itself, which its own API reaches without the crate's doing |
| `behaviour` | no undefined behaviour: a panic, a wrong value, a swallowed error, a leak, or a divergence from the C or the specification |
| `nit` | nothing a consumer can observe: a missing or imprecise `// SAFETY:` justification, an under-documented `# Safety` obligation that no reproducer breaks, or an API-shape finding of `unsafety`, `ergonomics`, `idiom` or `conventions` |

What only misuse can reach is not reportable and gets no report: a private item no public
API reaches with the inputs in question, or an `unsafe` API called against its stated
obligations.

### 1.3 Root causes

A report is one root cause. Sites that share a defect are one report that lists them,
whatever objective or instrument met each. Before a finding is filed, the reports already
in the tree are searched for its cause, by site and mechanism, not by name: one a batch
of its own filed takes the new site; one another batch filed is named in `same-cause`.

### 1.4 Notes

Outside a Crustify-generated crate, a `nit` gets no report directory: it is one line, with
its site, in the batch's `notes.md` at the root of its reviews dir, grouped by kind, such
as unjustified `unsafe` blocks. So is a candidate that reading supports and no true
reproducer can show, as `unproven`, with why none is possible. A campaign keeps one such
note per crate, merged from its batches'.

## 2. Reproducers

A `ub`, `equiv` or `logic` candidate becomes a finding only once a reproducer proves it,
and so does a `contracts` candidate that claims a contract can be broken. A contract that
merely asks for more than the implementation needs, or a missing justification, is a
finding without one.

- A UB reproducer triggers one of the available sanitizers from Rust, and its report
  carries the sanitizer's trace. One targeting the safe public API carries
  `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; one targeting the unsafe API, or breaking a contract, honours
  the `# Safety` obligation, and its report says, for each `unsafe` it writes, why the
  defect is still the crate's. One reaching an export calls it as C would, through its
  raw binding, within the C declaration's contract.
- An equivalence reproducer fails one of [`testing`](../../testing/SKILL.md)'s equivalence
  comparisons while running the raw C and the public Rust API, and its report carries the
  failing assertion. Once the C is gone, a behaviour finding is a `logic` one.
- A logic reproducer fails a Rust assertion of what the specification it cites requires,
  and its report carries the failing assertion.

Each reproducer is a standalone Cargo package: its `Cargo.toml` declares an empty
`[workspace]` table and depends on the affected crate through a relative `path`, and its
`src/main.rs` runs one scenario, so that running it exits non-zero on the affected commit.

Whatever its kind, a reproducer is a true proof of concept:

- it links the affected crate itself and reaches the defect through its public API: it
  copies none of the crate's code, a private module included, and stands in for no part
  of the crate or of the C with a stub or a model;
- it is deterministic: every run gives the same verdict, and one that depends on an
  interleaving runs under the sanitizer that reports the race whichever thread wins;
- it fails visibly, for the reason its report states, and would pass were the defect
  absent: a comparison that passes, or a failure of the reproducer's own setup, proves
  nothing; and
- it is minimal: one scenario, with nothing the failure does not need.

## 3. Disclosure

# The provisional lesson `cmake-property-naming-a-removed-source` takes in the switch that removes a directory's last source

**Where.** `crustify/LESSONS.md`, `cmake-property-naming-a-removed-source`, added on
2026-11-14 from `module-switch-procedure`'s item 13: its Scope, "the switches of
`deps/llhttp/*.c`", and its last sentence, "The dangling name stays until the last file the
property names goes".

**What is wrong.** The rule (leave a `CMakeLists.txt` that names the removed source only in
a source-file property unchanged) holds for `api.c`'s and `http.c`'s switches, as its
evidence shows: gen3 and gen5 configured and built, and gen5's `build.ninja` in every variant
still compiles `llhttp.c` with the property's flags. Its scope also takes in
`deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s switch, the directory's last C source. There the directory's
`file(GLOB SRC_LLHTTP "*.c" "*.h")` leaves `llhttp.h` alone, `add_library(llhttp OBJECT …)`
has nothing to compile, and CMake fails to generate. That switch must edit CMake, which the
rule says no switch in its scope does. The lesson it extends, "A libgit2 module's switch
removes its file from `c/` and changes no CMake file" (scope: every later module's switch),
has the same gap, at the switch that removes any directory's last source. That entry is not
provisional, so it is left for the next reconciliation of the lessons.

**Reproduce.**

```
d=$(mktemp -d) && git -C c archive 230c9dbdb | tar -x -C $d && cp -r $d $d-drop && rm $d-drop/deps/llhttp/llhttp.c
for s in $d $d-drop; do cmake -S $s -B $s-b -G Ninja -DUSE_HTTPS=OpenSSL -DUSE_SHA1=builtin \
  -DUSE_SHA256=HTTPS -DUSE_HTTP_PARSER=builtin -DUSE_SSH=OFF -DBUILD_TESTS=OFF -DBUILD_CLI=OFF \
  -DLIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY=/nonexistent.a; echo "rc=$?"; done
```

The copy as it is configures (`rc=0`); the copy without `llhttp.c` fails (`rc=1`):
`CMake Error: CMake can not determine linker language for target: llhttp`.

**Fix.** The entry's rule now says the dangling names stay while the directory keeps a C
source, and that the switch removing its last one is outside the rule and edits CMake. Its
scope is narrowed to switches after which the directory keeps a C source, `api.c`'s and
`http.c`'s here, and excludes `llhttp.c`'s. The evidence cites this check. Changed, the entry
stays `provisional`, for the next review batch. Its generality is as before: it refines a
libgit2-specific lesson (libgit2's CMake globs each directory's sources), and the general
gate is `switch-gate-beyond-c-tests`'s, not this.

**Tiers.** Caught by this review batch, the first to read the lesson; no earlier tier had it.
EOF

# The provisional lesson `http-exports-gated-through-a-local-remote` miscounts the gate's failing clones

**Where.** `crustify/LESSONS.md`, `http-exports-gated-through-a-local-remote`, its rule: "It
runs a variant's `git2 clone` of two repositories through each framing, three clones that
fail, and `libgit2_tests …`".

**What is wrong.** `http-gate.sh` has run four failing clones since it was added
(`testrepo-close`, `testrepo-malformed`, `missing`, `unauthorised`), and its successful clones
and `libgit2_tests` runs go through three framings, `length`, `chunked` and `chunked-ext`, not
"each framing": `close` and `malformed` are framings of the failing clones. A switch that
followed the rule as written would expect three failing-clone lines and find four. The rest
of the entry holds: no offline C test drives the HTTP client (the module pass's finding);
the procedure (old generation beside new on plain, ASan+UBSan and TSan, `results.txt`
compared with `diff`, exports called counted on the coverage variant) is what both switches
ran; its general form is the open proposal `switch-gate-beyond-c-tests`, which answers the
generality test; and its scope names the modules whose exports only the HTTP client reaches.

**Reproduce.**

```
for c in 0c1bd7a0d 46055d7c3; do git show $c:crustify/scripts/http-gate.sh | grep -c '^clone .* fail$'; done   # 4, 4
grep -c '^clone .* rc=128' crustify/artifacts/modules/libgit2/deps/llhttp/http.c/integration/run-1/http-gate-results.txt   # 4
```

**Fix.** The rule names the three framings libgit2 reads to their end and the four failing
clones, and says `libgit2_tests` runs through each of the three; the evidence cites the
check. Changed, the entry stays `provisional`, for the next review batch.

**Tiers.** Caught by this review batch, the first to read the lesson; no earlier tier had it.

# The provisional lesson `cmake-property-naming-a-removed-source` takes in the switch that removes a directory's last source

**Where.** `crustify/LESSONS.md`, `cmake-property-naming-a-removed-source`, added on
2026-11-14 from `module-switch-procedure`'s item 13: its Scope, "the switches of
`deps/llhttp/*.c`", and its last sentence, "The dangling name stays until the last file the
property names goes".

**What is wrong.** The rule (leave a `CMakeLists.txt` that names the removed source only in
a source-file property unchanged) holds for `api.c`'s and `http.c`'s switches, as its
evidence shows: gen3 and gen5 configured and built, and gen5's `build.ninja` in every variant
still compiles `llhttp.c` with the property's flags. Its scope also takes in
`deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s switch, the directory's last C source. There the directory's
`file(GLOB SRC_LLHTTP "*.c" "*.h")` leaves `llhttp.h` alone, `add_library(llhttp OBJECT …)`
has nothing to compile, and CMake fails to generate. That switch must edit CMake, which the
rule says no switch in its scope does. The lesson it extends, "A libgit2 module's switch
removes its file from `c/` and changes no CMake file" (scope: every later module's switch),
has the same gap, at the switch that removes any directory's last source. That entry is not
provisional, so it is left for the next reconciliation of the lessons.

**Reproduce.**

`CMake Error: CMake can not determine linker language for target: llhttp`.

source, and that the switch removing its last one is outside the rule and edits CMake. Its
scope is narrowed to switches after which the directory keeps a C source, `api.c`'s and
`http.c`'s here, and excludes `llhttp.c`'s. The evidence cites this check. Changed, the entry
stays `provisional`, for the next review batch. Its generality is as before: it refines a
libgit2-specific lesson (libgit2's CMake globs each directory's sources), and the general
gate is `switch-gate-beyond-c-tests`'s, not this.

    def env(self, stage: str, **extra: str) -> dict[str, str]:

            env.setdefault("CARGO_TARGET_DIR", str(self.snap / "target" / "miri"))
        env.update(self.stage_env.get(stage, {}))
